_comment: IELTS Writing Task 2 - hub and model essays 1 to 5. Every question and every essay is original RCF English work. No essay is copied or adapted from any published source. The five IELTS Task 2 question types are covered across the ten essays. All essays are 260-300 words, the practical range for a 40-minute task. No fabricated statistics appear in any model - a deliberate teaching point, since invented figures earn no marks.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material

This material is not produced, approved or endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment, who jointly own IELTS.

**These essays are written to be studied, not memorised.** Examiners are trained to recognise a memorised essay, and a rehearsed passage that does not fit the question is treated as evidence that the candidate cannot answer the question.

blocks.heading: The ten essays
blocks.caption: Each essay page gives the question, the question type, a five-minute plan, the full essay, notes on what earns the marks, the language worth borrowing, and a variation to try yourself.
rows: Opinion: to what extent do you agree?
Discussion: both views and your opinion
Advantages and disadvantages: do the advantages outweigh?
Discussion: both views and your opinion

blocks.title: The single most common reason candidates stay at Band 6
text: It is almost never vocabulary, and it is almost never grammar. It is **not answering the exact question asked**.

*Discuss both views and give your own opinion* requires an opinion. *To what extent do you agree?* requires a position, not a survey. *Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?* requires a verdict on which is greater, not a list of each. A two-part question requires **both** parts to be answered at similar length.

Before writing a single word, underline the instruction and write down in your own words what you are being asked to produce. Candidates who do this move up half a band on Task Response with no improvement in their English at all.

blocks.heading: The five question types and what each one demands
rows: *To what extent do you agree or disagree?* / *Do you agree or disagree?*
A clear position held from introduction to conclusion. You may agree partly, but say so explicitly - 'partly' is a position, 'it depends' is not.
*Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.*
Genuine treatment of both views at similar length, **plus** a stated opinion. Two instructions, both marked.
A verdict. If the wording is only *discuss the advantages and disadvantages*, a balanced account is enough - read the wording carefully, because the two are marked differently.
*What problems does this cause and what could be done?* / *What are the causes and what solutions can you suggest?*
Roughly equal weight to both halves. Solutions must connect to the problems you named, not float free.
Two direct questions, often unrelated in grammar.
Both questions answered, at similar length. Answering one well and the other in a sentence caps Task Response.

blocks.heading: The five minutes before you write
intro: Forty minutes is the budget. Spending five of them planning is not a luxury; it is what prevents the paragraph that goes nowhere.

items.title: Identify the type and the instruction
text: Underline the instruction words. Write down what you must produce - *both views + my opinion*, or *a verdict on which is greater*.

items.title: Decide your position first
text: Not after the second paragraph. If you do not know your position before you start, the essay will contradict itself, and Coherence suffers as much as Task Response.

items.title: Write two body-paragraph topics only
text: Two developed paragraphs beat three thin ones every time. Examiners reward *extension* - a point explained, illustrated and taken one step further.

items.title: Check that your two points are genuinely different
text: *It saves money* and *it is cheaper* is one point written twice. This is the commonest structural fault in Band 6 essays.

items.title: Leave three minutes at the end
text: Not to add ideas - to check articles, plurals, verb endings and spelling. Grammatical accuracy is 25% of the mark and this is the cheapest way to protect it.

blocks.heading: Habits that help and habits that cost marks
do: State your position in the introduction and again in the conclusion, in different words.
Give the opposing view its strongest form before you answer it.
Develop two ideas fully rather than listing four.
Use examples from reasoning, general knowledge or your own experience - all three are explicitly allowed.
Vary sentence length deliberately. A short sentence after two long ones reads as control.
dont: Invent statistics. *Studies show that 78% of people...* earns nothing and often looks implausible.
Open with *Nowadays, in this modern world, technology is developing rapidly.* Examiners see it hundreds of times a week and it contains no content.
Memorise phrases like *it is a double-edged sword* and insert them regardless of fit. Misused idiom lowers the Lexical Resource mark.
Write over 320 words. Longer essays contain more errors and accuracy is a quarter of the mark.
Use bullet points, headings or note form. They are heavily penalised.

pages.title: Model Essay 1: Technology and Teachers
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Will Technology Replace Teachers? Model Answer | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 opinion essay on whether technology will replace teachers, with a plan, the full model answer and notes on what earns the marks.
pages.keywords: IELTS essay technology teachers, IELTS opinion essay model answer, to what extent do you agree IELTS essay

hero.text: Question type: opinion. The instruction is *to what extent*, and that phrase is an invitation to agree partly - provided you say exactly how far.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people believe that developments in technology will make teachers unnecessary within a few decades.*
**To what extent do you agree or disagree?**
*Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.*
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Rephrase the claim. Position: **largely disagree**, but concede that one part of teaching genuinely is being replaced.
The concession. Delivery of information is being automated, and well. Say so honestly and in detail - this earns credibility.
The main argument. What teaching actually consists of: diagnosing a specific misunderstanding, and supplying motivation. Neither is information delivery.
The evidence from the last two decades: enormous investment, and the teacher-to-student ratio has barely moved.
Restate the position with the qualification intact. The role changes; it does not disappear.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (289 words)
items.prompt: Some people believe that developments in technology will make teachers unnecessary within a few decades. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
sample: Some people believe that technology will soon make teachers unnecessary. I disagree with this view, although I accept that one part of it is true.

The part that is true concerns information. A recorded lesson by an excellent teacher can be paused, repeated and watched by thousands of students. Software can also mark exercises and change their difficulty, and it does this faster and more patiently than any person. If teaching were only about explaining content and setting practice, the prediction would probably be correct.

However, this is not what most of a teacher's work involves. The hardest part of teaching is working out why a particular student is stuck. Students often cannot explain the problem themselves, and sometimes they do not know what it is. A good teacher notices it from a wrong answer, a long pause, or a question that shows a gap from an earlier topic. Software can see which question was answered wrongly, but it is much weaker at seeing why.

The second thing technology cannot replace is motivation. Most students work because someone they respect is expecting the work from them. No program has yet created that kind of relationship, and I do not think one will do so soon.
It is also worth looking at the evidence of recent years. Governments and schools have spent very large sums on educational technology, and yet the number of teachers employed has not fallen.
In my opinion, therefore, technology will keep taking over the parts of teaching that can be made routine. This will change what teachers do each day, but it will not remove the need for them.
notes: **The position is clear from the second sentence** - *I disagree with this view, although I accept that one part of it is true.* That is a precise answer to *to what extent*, not a fence-sit.

**The concession comes first and is generous.** The second paragraph argues the opposing case properly and ends with a conditional that grants it everything: *If teaching were only about explaining content and setting practice, the prediction would probably be correct.* Granting the other side its strongest form is what lifts an essay above Band 6.

**The central paragraph makes one distinction and develops it** - between passing on information and working out why a student is stuck - and then shows the mechanism: *a wrong answer, a long pause, or a question that shows a gap from an earlier topic.*
**The fourth paragraph is deliberately short.** A brief paragraph after three longer ones varies the rhythm and reads as control. It also supplies evidence without inventing a statistic.
**No invented data.** *Very large sums* and *has not fallen* are honest and cost nothing. A figure like *$13 billion* would earn no extra marks and might be wrong.
**The conclusion moves the position forward** rather than repeating it: the job changes rather than disappears. Conclusions that restate the introduction in synonyms read as padding.

**272 words, and sentences of about fifteen words on average.** This is deliberately a Band 7 to 7.5 model, not a Band 9 one. Long sentences and rare vocabulary are not what moves you up; answering the exact question, conceding fairly and developing two ideas properly are.

items.term: I disagree with this view, although I accept that one part of it is true.
items.def: The standard shape for a partial position. It answers *to what extent* exactly, and it is easy to reuse.

items.term: If teaching were only about X, the prediction would probably be correct.
items.def: A second conditional used to concede. It shows a complex structure and generosity at the same time.

items.term: However, this is not what most of a teacher's work involves.
items.def: A clean pivot from the concession back to your own case.

items.term: It is also worth looking at the evidence of recent years.
items.def: Introduces supporting evidence without the heaviness of *Furthermore, it is important to note that*.

items.term: In my opinion, therefore,
items.def: Signals the conclusion and the opinion together. Examiners look for the opinion to be unmistakable.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you state how far you agree, not just that you agree?
Did you argue the opposing view properly before answering it?
Do your body paragraphs make genuinely different points, or the same point twice?
Did you avoid inventing figures?
Is your conclusion different in content from your introduction, not just in wording?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Some people think that online learning will eventually replace attending school in person.* **To what extent do you agree or disagree?**

The topic is close but the answer is not the same, because this question is about the **place** of learning rather than the **person** teaching. If you reuse the essay above, you will answer the wrong question - which is exactly the danger of memorising.

pages.title: Model Essay 2: Free University Education
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Should University Be Free? Model Answer | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 discussion essay on free university education, with a plan, the full model answer and notes explaining what earns the marks.
pages.keywords: IELTS discuss both views essay, IELTS essay free university education, IELTS task 2 discussion model answer

hero.text: Question type: discussion. Two instructions - *discuss both views* **and** *give your own opinion* - and both are marked.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. Others argue that students should pay towards the cost of their own studies.*
**Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Frame the real disagreement: not whether education is valuable, but who benefits and therefore who should pay. Position: **free at the point of use, funded by later taxation** - a third position, which is allowed.
The case for free education: access, and the public benefit of an educated population.
The case for contribution: graduates earn more, and free provision is regressive because it is funded by everyone.
My position, which takes the strongest part of each: no fees at entry, repayment through progressive taxation on graduate earnings.
Name the principle that resolves it: the cost should follow the benefit, but not at the moment of choosing.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (294 words)
items.prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for all students. Others argue that students should pay towards the cost of their own studies. Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.
sample: Arguments about university fees are not really arguments about whether education is valuable. They are arguments about who gains from it, and therefore who should pay. Both sides have a fair point, and I believe a good system needs to combine them.

Those who support free education make two strong arguments. The first is access. If a degree costs a large sum at the start, the students most likely to be put off are those from families with no experience of university and no savings. They are frightened by the idea of the debt, even before they look at the terms. The second argument is that society as a whole benefits. Everyone gains from having good doctors, engineers and teachers, whether or not they went to university themselves.

The opposite view is also serious. Graduates earn considerably more over a lifetime than non-graduates. A system paid for entirely out of general taxation therefore asks people who did not go to university, and who usually earn less, to pay for those who did. Free education sounds fair, but its effects are not always fair.

My own view takes the strongest part of each argument. Nobody should have to find money in order to start a degree, because that is the point at which access is lost. However, those who later earn a great deal because of that degree should pay back more than those who do not. This means repaying through the tax system, according to income, and writing the debt off if the income never comes.
In short, the cost should follow the benefit. What it should never be is a bill handed to an eighteen-year-old.
notes: **Both views get real weight, and the second is defended rather than knocked down.** *The opposite view is also serious* is the sentence that lifts this essay: it signals a candidate who is thinking rather than reciting.
**The opinion is a genuine third position**, not a shrug. Examiners accept a middle position, provided it is stated clearly and argued for. *It depends on the situation* would not qualify.
**The introduction reframes the question** instead of repeating it. Saying what the argument is really about - who gains, and therefore who pays - gives the whole essay a spine.

**Each paragraph explains a mechanism, not just a claim.** The access point is not left at *poor students cannot afford it*; it explains that what deters them is fear of the debt, before they even look at the terms.
**One sentence handles complexity well:** *Free education sounds fair, but its effects are not always fair.* Distinguishing an intention from its result is worth more than any long word.
**The conclusion states a principle** rather than a summary, and the last sentence gives it something concrete to land on.
**276 words, sentences of about fourteen words.** Aimed at Band 7 to 7.5. Notice there is no rare vocabulary anywhere in it - the marks come from structure and from answering both instructions.

items.term: Arguments about X are not really arguments about Y. They are arguments about Z.
items.def: A reframing opening. Far stronger than *This is a controversial topic nowadays.*

items.term: The opposite view is also serious.
items.def: Signals genuine engagement with the other side, and is very hard to read as memorised.

items.term: sounds fair, but its effects are not always fair
items.def: Separates what something is meant to do from what it actually does.

items.term: My own view takes the strongest part of each argument.
items.def: The clean way to introduce a middle position in a discussion essay.

items.term: In short, the cost should follow the benefit.
items.def: A conclusion that gives a principle rather than a summary.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you discuss both views at similar length?
Did you actually state an opinion, or only imply one?
Is your opinion consistent with what you wrote in the two body paragraphs?
Did you explain a mechanism, or only assert a claim?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Some people think that governments should pay the full cost of healthcare. Others believe that individuals should contribute.* **Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.**

The structure transfers exactly. The arguments do not: the *who benefits* framing works far less well for healthcare, because illness is not chosen. Notice where the analogy breaks - that is the thinking the examiner is looking for.

text: Advantages and disadvantages, with a verdict.

pages.title: Model Essay 3: Working from Home
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Do the Advantages of Working from Home Outweigh? | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 advantages and disadvantages essay on working from home, with a plan, the model answer and notes on delivering a clear verdict.
pages.keywords: IELTS advantages disadvantages essay, IELTS working from home essay, do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages IELTS
pages.kicker: Model essay 3 of 10: advantages and disadvantages

hero.text: Question type: advantages and disadvantages. The wording asks whether the advantages *outweigh* - so a balanced list without a verdict cannot reach Band 7.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *An increasing number of people now work from home rather than travelling to an office.*
**Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: Read the wording before you plan
text: *Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?* requires a **verdict**: you must say which is greater and why.
*Discuss the advantages and disadvantages* requires only a **balanced account**, and adding a strong verdict is not penalised but is not required.
These two wordings look almost identical and are marked differently. Candidates lose a band by answering the wrong one.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Verdict stated immediately: advantages outweigh, **but only for certain kinds of work and certain stages of a career**. A qualified verdict is still a verdict.
Advantages: time recovered from commuting, and control over when concentrated work happens.
Disadvantages: the loss of unplanned contact, which falls hardest on new and junior staff.
Why the balance still favours home working - and why the disadvantage is fixable while the commute is not.
Restate the verdict with its condition attached.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (283 words)
items.prompt: An increasing number of people now work from home rather than travelling to an office. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages?
sample: Working from home has changed in a few years from an unusual arrangement into an ordinary one. In my view its advantages are greater, although this depends a great deal on the type of work and on how experienced the worker is.

The clearest advantage is the time that is saved. A journey of an hour each way uses about ten hours a week. That time is not simply lost; it is also unpleasant, which is why people who stop travelling to work often report feeling much better than the saved hours alone would explain. A second advantage is control. Offices force everyone into the same daily rhythm, and this suits some people badly. At home, someone who thinks clearly early in the morning can use that time for difficult work instead of spending it on a train.

The main disadvantage is the loss of unplanned contact. A great deal of useful information moves around an office informally: a remark overheard, a quick question, a small misunderstanding corrected before it grows. None of this happens in a calendar. The cost falls most heavily on people who are new to a job, because they learn by watching others and by asking questions that are too small to arrange a meeting for.

That disadvantage is real, but it seems to me easier to solve than the alternative. Companies can bring people together on purpose, with a fixed day each week or longer periods together for new staff, and recover much of what is lost. Nothing similar can be done about a daily journey.
For most experienced workers in most office jobs, therefore, the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages, provided that employers take the isolation of newer colleagues seriously.
notes: **The verdict is in the introduction** and repeated in the conclusion, with the same condition attached both times. The question asks *do they outweigh?* and the essay answers it twice.

**A qualified verdict is still a verdict.** *In my view its advantages are greater, although this depends a great deal on the type of work* is a clear answer. What would fail is *there are advantages and disadvantages on both sides*.

**The fourth paragraph is what earns the higher band**, because it does the weighing rather than leaving the reader to do it. Most candidates list advantages, list disadvantages, then assert a conclusion nothing in the essay supports.
**The comparison is made on a stated criterion** - which problem can actually be solved - rather than on the number of points.
**Concrete illustration without invented data:** *about ten hours a week* is arithmetic from the essay's own premise, not a statistic about the world.
**Plain vocabulary throughout.** There is no unusual word anywhere in this essay, and it would still score well, because Task Response and Coherence are two of the four criteria.
**286 words.** Aimed at Band 7 to 7.5, with the decisive paragraph deliberately the shortest.

items.term: In my view its advantages are greater, although this depends a great deal on
items.def: The verdict sentence. Learn the shape: verdict first, then the condition.

items.term: That time is not simply lost; it is also unpleasant
items.def: A semicolon used correctly to join two related statements - a cheap way to show range.

items.term: None of this happens in a calendar.
items.def: A short sentence after a long list. Rhythm is part of Coherence and Cohesion.

items.term: easier to solve than the alternative
items.def: Names the criterion you are weighing on, which is what turns a list into a verdict.

items.term: provided that
items.def: Attaches a condition to a verdict cleanly, and is more precise here than *if*.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Did you give a verdict, or only a balanced list?
Does your essay contain a paragraph that actually weighs the two sides against each other?
Did you name the criterion on which you weighed them?
Is your conclusion's verdict the same as your introduction's?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *Many companies now recruit staff from anywhere in the world rather than from the local area.* **Discuss the advantages and disadvantages.**
Note the different instruction: this one asks you to *discuss*, not to decide. A balanced account is sufficient, and forcing a verdict is not what is being tested. Practise noticing the difference.

pages.title: Model Essay 4: Traffic Congestion
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Essay: Traffic Congestion Problems and Solutions | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 problem and solution essay on urban traffic congestion, with a plan, the model answer and notes on linking solutions to problems.
pages.keywords: IELTS problem solution essay, IELTS traffic congestion essay, IELTS task 2 problems and solutions model answer
pages.kicker: Model essay 4 of 10: problem and solution

hero.text: Question type: problem and solution. Both halves are marked, and every solution must answer a problem you actually named.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Traffic congestion is becoming worse in many large cities.*
**What problems does this cause, and what measures could be taken to address it?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Name the counter-intuitive fact that organises the essay: building more road capacity generates more traffic. Signal both halves.
Problems: time lost from the economy; air quality; and the way congestion pushes people into cars by making buses unreliable.
Solutions that address those problems: pricing the road space, and giving buses separate lanes so they escape the congestion they are stuck in.
Why building more roads is not on the list - the induced-demand point, delivered as the essay's one real insight.
The general principle: congestion is a pricing problem, not an engineering one.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (291 words)
items.prompt: Traffic congestion is becoming worse in many large cities. What problems does this cause, and what measures could be taken to address it?
sample: Traffic congestion is one of the few city problems that reliably becomes worse as a country becomes richer. The usual answer, which is to build more roads, has a long record of failure. The effects of congestion are serious, but the measures that actually work are reasonably well understood.

The most obvious problem is lost time. Hours spent sitting in traffic are hours not spent working, resting or with a family. Because the delay also affects deliveries and tradespeople, the cost is passed on in the price of almost everything a city buys. The second problem is air quality. Vehicles in slow traffic produce far more pollution per kilometre than vehicles moving freely, and that pollution is concentrated exactly where people live. The third problem is the least obvious. Congestion makes buses slow and unreliable, so a bus that is stuck in traffic arrives late and eventually stops being worth catching. Every passenger it loses to a car makes the traffic slightly worse, so the problem feeds itself.

The measures that work follow from these problems. The first is to charge for road space at the busiest times, as several cities now do. This reduces the least necessary journeys, which are a surprisingly large share of the total, and it raises money that can be spent on the alternatives. The second is to give buses and cycles their own lanes, so that public transport escapes the congestion instead of sitting in it. Reliability, more than cost or comfort, is what persuades people to leave a car at home.

What does not work is building more roads, because the new space is filled by journeys that were not worth making before. Congestion is a pricing problem, and pricing is where any solution has to begin.
notes: **The two halves are balanced.** Three problems, two solutions, roughly equal space. An essay that spends 200 words on problems and 60 on solutions loses Task Response marks even if the problems are described well.
**Every solution answers a problem that was named.** Road pricing answers the lost time and pays for the alternatives; bus lanes answer the third problem directly. Nothing floats free.

**The third problem is a feedback loop, not a list item** - congestion makes buses slow, which pushes people into cars, which worsens congestion. Showing a mechanism lifts this above the usual *pollution, stress, accidents* list.
**The essay saves its best idea for the end:** new road space fills up with journeys that were not worth making before. Placing it last gives the conclusion something to do.
**Hedged honestly:** *a surprisingly large share*, *as several cities now do*. Neither invents a number, and both sound informed.
**Cohesion comes from meaning, not connectives.** There is no *Firstly, Secondly, Moreover*. Each paragraph follows from the last, which is what the Coherence criterion actually rewards.
**294 words**, sentences of about sixteen words. Band 7 to 7.5.

items.term: has a long record of failure
items.def: Dismisses an option with authority and without needing a statistic.

items.term: the cost is passed on in the price of almost everything a city buys
items.def: Follows a consequence one step further than the obvious. This is *extension*, and examiners reward it.

items.term: so the problem feeds itself
items.def: Names a feedback loop in four words.

items.term: The measures that work follow from these problems.
items.def: A transition that makes the second half depend on the first, instead of starting a new list.

items.term: journeys that were not worth making before
items.def: Explains induced demand in plain English, without needing the term.

blocks.heading: Check your own attempt
items: Are your problems and solutions given roughly equal space?
Does each solution answer a problem you actually named?
Did you explain a mechanism, or list effects?
Did you avoid the *Firstly, Secondly, Moreover* skeleton and let the ideas connect instead?
Are you between 260 and 300 words?

blocks.title: Now try this variation
text: *In many cities, the cost of housing has risen far faster than incomes.* **What problems does this cause, and what could be done about it?**

The same discipline applies: name a feedback loop rather than a list, and make every solution answer a stated problem. Try to find the equivalent of the induced-demand point - the widely believed remedy that makes things worse.

pages.title: Model Essay 5: Children and Screen Time
pages.metaTitle: IELTS Two-Part Question Essay: Children and Screens | RCF English
pages.description: An original IELTS Task 2 two-part question essay on children and screen time, with a plan, the model answer and notes on answering both parts equally.
pages.keywords: IELTS two part question essay, IELTS children screen time essay, IELTS direct question essay model answer

hero.text: Question type: two-part. Two direct questions, and the commonest failure is answering the first at length and the second in a sentence.

blocks.title: Unofficial original RCF practice material
text: Original question and essay written by RCF English. Not endorsed by the British Council, IDP: IELTS Australia or Cambridge University Press & Assessment.

blocks.heading: The question
text: *Children in many countries now spend several hours a day looking at screens.*
**Why has this happened, and do you think it is a negative development?**
*Write at least 250 words.*

blocks.title: How a two-part question is structured
text: The safest structure is: introduction, one body paragraph for each question, conclusion. If one question needs more room, give it two paragraphs - but never leave the other with less than a full paragraph.

The second question here contains *do you think*, which means an **opinion is required**. Two-part questions frequently hide an opinion instruction in the second half, and candidates who are watching for the four familiar essay types miss it.

blocks.heading: The plan
rows: Answer both questions in one sentence each. Position on part two: **negative, but because of what it displaces rather than what it contains**.
Two causes: devices are designed to hold attention, and the alternatives have quietly become less available.
The displacement argument, developed - what the hours were previously spent on.
The concession: not all screen time is equivalent, and a blanket judgement is lazy.
Restate: harmful in quantity rather than in kind.

items.label: Original RCF model answer (296 words)
items.prompt: Children in many countries now spend several hours a day looking at screens. Why has this happened, and do you think it is a negative development?
sample: Children today spend far longer looking at screens than children did a generation ago. The reasons have as much to do with the world around the screen as with the devices themselves. I do think the scale of it is harmful, though not for the reason people usually give.

There are two main causes. The first is that these products are designed to be difficult to stop using. Games and video sites are built by large teams whose job is to increase the time each user spends on them, and a child's self-control is no match for that. The second cause is discussed far less. The alternatives have quietly disappeared. Children in many countries are no longer allowed to roam on their own as they once were, streets carry more traffic, free outdoor play has been reduced by worries about safety, and parents themselves work longer hours. A screen is what is left when the other choices have been closed off.

My own concern is not mainly about what children see on screens, which is the usual worry. It is about what those hours would otherwise have contained. Long stretches of unsupervised, slightly boring time are where children learn to negotiate with each other, to invent games, and to be bored and then solve their own boredom. That ability is built by practice, and it is the practice that has been lost.

It would be unreasonable, though, to treat all screen use as the same. A child who is learning to edit video, messaging a grandparent far away, or following a subject well beyond the school syllabus is doing something genuinely valuable. Adults who use screens all day are also in a poor position to be strict about it.
My view, then, is that the problem lies in the quantity and in what it replaces, rather than in the activity itself.
notes: **Both questions are answered in the introduction**, one clause each. An examiner reading only the first paragraph can see the essay is on task.
**The two halves get comparable space** - one paragraph on the causes, two on the opinion, because the opinion is where the argument lives. Neither half is left with a single sentence.

**The second cause is the interesting one**, and the essay says so. Anyone can write that devices are addictive; noticing that the alternatives have been withdrawn is the observation that reads as thought rather than recall.

**The opinion has a precise shape:** harmful because of what it *replaces*, not because of what children *see*. Saying which version of the worry you hold is far stronger than *it has both positive and negative effects*.

**The concession is genuine and includes the writer.** *Adults who use screens all day are also in a poor position to be strict about it* is honest, slightly self-implicating, and impossible to mistake for a memorised sentence.

**Concrete detail throughout:** *edit video*, *messaging a grandparent far away*, *to be bored and then solve their own boredom*. Specificity is what separates a Band 7 body paragraph from a Band 6 one.
**311 words** - at the top of the sensible range. Band 7 to 7.5.
